title: Kabir: the death that delights
hookLine: the death the world fears fills Kabir with joy, for it brings the Beloved near (Kabir salok, ang 1365)

cards: There's a whole vocabulary for not saying it: passed away, lost, gone. The subject gets changed. Nobody puts it on the calendar.
That's human; it's a frightening thing. Then there's an old weaver who, when the subject comes up, doesn't flinch. He leans in.
He says the thing the world is afraid of makes his heart glad. Not because he's tired of life. Because of who he thinks is waiting.

teach.h: WHAT THE WORLD FEARS, KABIR WELCOMES.
teach.b: Among Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1365: kabeer jis marne te jag darai mere man aanand; marne hee te paaeeai pooran parmaanand.
Kabir, the death the world is so afraid of fills my mind with bliss; for it's through dying that one finds perfect, supreme joy.

Aanand is joy, the same word as the Anand Sahib; parmaanand is supreme joy. Why joy? Remember the bride from day two hundred forty-four, waiting for her beloved, and Sohila's wedding date, already written.
Kabir stands in that same picture.

teach.h: DIE BEFORE YOU DIE: THE EGO.
teach.b: If the soul is a bride longing for God, the day of meeting isn't a disaster. It's the day she's been waiting for. There's a second layer.
Kabir, and the Gurus after him, often speak of dying while alive: letting the ego die, the proud little I called haumai.
In another salok, in paraphrase, Kabir says the whole world keeps dying, yet nobody knows how to die; die the kind of death after which you never die again.
Some readers hear in it the death of ego, which frees a person to live without fear. Tradition adds a story people tell.
A popular belief held that dying in Kashi, Benares, brought liberation, and dying in the town of Maghar did not.
Kabir, it's said, went to Maghar to die, to show that it's the heart, not the place.
In one hymn he says himself that at the end he left for Maghar; in another, that Kashi and Maghar are the same to one who has God in the heart.

how: Kabir's saloks are read in the Guru Granth Sahib and quoted in Sikh reflections on death, where Sikh teaching discourages loud mourning and speaks of death as the soul's return.

o: a Bhagat who met death with joy, not fear
a poet who wrote mourning songs for funerals
a holy man who chose to die in holy Kashi

games.q: inside Kabir's salok — tap the pairs.
p: where Kabir went to die, it's said

s: Kabir's salok says death should be dreaded
the death the world fears fills his mind with joy.
Kabir and the Gurus speak of dying while alive, the death of ego
die the death after which you never die again.
Kabir's hymns say where you die matters most
his hymns say Kashi and Maghar are the same to one with God in the heart.

games.q: a popular belief says dying in Benares brings liberation. the story says Kabir is near death. where does he go?
o: to Maghar, a town people thought unlucky, to show it's the heart that matters.
nowhere: he refuses to speak of it.
games.why: tradition says Kabir went to Maghar; his hymns say Kashi and Maghar are the same to the one who has God in the heart.

practice: Name one fear, small or large: a test result, a hard conversation, a change that's coming. Let it sit beside you like someone on the same bench; you don't have to argue with it or send it away.
Notice the breath still coming and going, and that you're still here, unhurried, the fear beside you rather than on top of you.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. Here, his salok: the death the world fears fills his heart with joy, for through it comes supreme bliss, the meeting with the Beloved.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: aanand, joy; the same word as the Anand Sahib, and here, Kabir's joy at meeting death.

carryVoice: Your line: what they fear, I welcome. For Kabir, it was a meeting, not an ending. Rest well; more Kabir tomorrow.
